html:
A Gothic palace on the Grand Canal in Venice, near the Rialto, built from 1421 to 1437 for the nobleman Marino Contarini. Its name, "House of Gold", comes from the gilding and colour once laid on its front. Contarini directed the work himself and his accounts survive. The stonework was by Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bon, who also made the Porta della Carta of the Doge's Palace, and by Matteo Raverti from Milan.

It has long been counted the best-surviving Venetian Gothic palace. The front is not symmetrical. At water level a loggia opens onto an entrance hall where goods were landed, as in other merchant houses. Above it two loggias of slender columns and quatrefoil tracery, a pattern taken from the Doge's Palace, front the main hall, and a crest of pinnacles runs along the roof. The stone was treated to look like marble, and in 1431 the painter Zoane di Franza gilded the details.

After the republic fell in 1797 the palace changed hands many times. Alessandro Trubetzkoi bought it in 1846 and gave it to the ballerina Marie Taglioni; the courtyard stair was torn out and the wellhead by Bartolomeo Bon sold. Baron Giorgio Franchetti bought the palace in 1894, recovered what he could, restored it, and in 1916 left it to the Italian state. It opened as a museum in 1927; its collection includes Mantegna's Saint Sebastian.
